arXiv:2010.06554v2 [math.PR] 05 May 2021

Singularity of Discrete Random Matrices

Vishesh Jain Address: Department of Statistics, Stanford University, Stanford, CA 94305, USA Email address: visheshj@stanford.edu , Ashwin Sah and Mehtaab Sawhney Address: Department of Mathematics, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA 02139, USA Email address: {asah,msawhney}@mit.edu
Abstract.

Let ξ\xi be a non-constant real-valued random variable with finite support, and let Mn​(ξ)M_{n}(\xi) denote an n×nn\times n random matrix with entries that are independent copies of ξ\xi.

For ξ\xi which is not uniform on its support, we show that

ℙ​[Mn​(ξ)​ is singular]\displaystyle\mathbb{P}[M_{n}(\xi)\text{ is singular}] =ℙ⁡[zero row or column]+(1+on​(1))​ℙ​[two equal (up to sign) rows or columns],\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}[\text{zero row or column}]+(1+o_{n}(1))\mathbb{P}[\text{two equal (up to sign) rows or columns}],

thereby confirming a folklore conjecture.

As special cases, we obtain:

  • •

    For ξ=Bernoulli⁡(p)\xi=\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p) with fixed p∈(0,1/2)p\in(0,1/2),

    ℙ⁡[Mn​(ξ)​ is singular]=2​n​(1−p)n+(1+on​(1))​n​(n−1)​(p2+(1−p)2)n,\mathbb{P}[M_{n}(\xi)\text{ is singular}]=2n(1-p)^{n}+(1+o_{n}(1))n(n-1)(p^{2}+(1-p)^{2})^{n},

    which determines the singularity probability to two asymptotic terms. Previously, no result of such precision was available in the study of the singularity of random matrices.

  • •

    For ξ=Bernoulli⁡(p)\xi=\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p) with fixed p∈(1/2,1)p\in(1/2,1),

    ℙ⁡[Mn​(ξ)​ is singular]=(1+on​(1))​n​(n−1)​(p2+(1−p)2)n.\mathbb{P}[M_{n}(\xi)\text{ is singular}]=(1+o_{n}(1))n(n-1)(p^{2}+(1-p)^{2})^{n}.

    Previously, only the much weaker upper bound of (p+on​(1))n(\sqrt{p}+o_{n}(1))^{n} was known due to the work of Bourgain-Vu-Wood.

For ξ\xi which is uniform on its support:

  • •

    We show that

    ℙ​[Mn​(ξ)​ is singular]\displaystyle\mathbb{P}[M_{n}(\xi)\text{ is singular}] =(1+on​(1))n​ℙ​[two rows or columns are equal].\displaystyle=(1+o_{n}(1))^{n}\mathbb{P}[\text{two rows or columns are equal}].
  • •

    Perhaps more importantly, we provide a sharp analysis of the contribution of the ‘compressible’ part of the unit sphere to the lower tail of the smallest singular value of Mn​(ξ)M_{n}(\xi).

1. Introduction

Let Mn​(ξ)M_{n}(\xi) be an n×nn\times n random matrix, each of whose entries is an independent copy of a random variable ξ\xi. We will restrict attention to when ξ\xi is a real-valued random variable whose support is finite and contains at least two points (which we call discrete). What is the probability that Mn​(ξ)M_{n}(\xi) is singular? This question, which has been studied since the 1960s, has attracted considerable attention over the years. A well-known folklore conjecture is that the dominant contribution to the probability of singularity is from the events that a row or column is zero, or that two rows or two columns are equal (possibly up to a sign). In order to facilitate discussion, let us introduce some notation. For a vector v∈ℝnv\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, we define the event

ℰv:={Mn(ξ)v=0}.\mathcal{E}_{v}:=\{M_{n}(\xi)v=0\}.

We will also denote the canonical basis vectors of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} by e1,…,ene_{1},\dots,e_{n}. Then, the aforementioned conjecture may be stated as follows.

Conjecture 1.1.

Let ξ\xi be a discrete random variable, and let Mn​(ξ)M_{n}(\xi) be an n×nn\times n random matrix whose entries are independent copies of ξ\xi. Then

ℙ⁡[Mn​(ξ)​​i​s​s​i​n​g​u​l​a​r]=(1+on​(1))​(2​n​ℙ​[ℰe1]+n⁡(n−1)​ℙ​[ℰe1−e2]+n⁡(n−1)​ℙ​[ℰe1+e2]).\mathbb{P}[M_{n}(\xi)\emph{issingular}]=(1+o_{n}(1))\bigg(2n\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{E}_{e_{1}}]+n(n-1)\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{E}_{e_{1}-e_{2}}]+n(n-1)\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{E}_{e_{1}+e_{2}}]\bigg).

In this paper, as our first main result, we confirm a stronger version of Conjecture 1.1 for all discrete distributions which are not uniform on their support. Let sn​(Mn)s_{n}(M_{n}) denote the least singular value of an n×nn\times n matrix MnM_{n}; recall that sn​(Mn)=infx∈𝕊n−1∥Mn​x∥2s_{n}(M_{n})=\inf_{x\in\mathbb{S}^{n-1}}\lVert M_{n}x\rVert_{2}, where 𝕊n−1\mathbb{S}^{n-1} denotes the unit sphere in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} and ∥⋅∥2\lVert\cdot\rVert_{2} denotes the standard Euclidean norm on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}.

Theorem 1.2.

Let ξ\xi be a discrete random variable which is not uniform on its support. There exist cξ,Cξ>0c_{\xi},C_{\xi}>0 so that for all sufficiently large nn, and for all t≥0t\geq 0,

ℙ[sn(Mn(ξ))≤t/n]≤Cξt+2nℙ[ℰe1]+(1+O(exp(−cξn)))(n(n−1)ℙ[ℰe1+e2]+n(n−1)ℙ[ℰe1−e2]).\mathbb{P}[s_{n}(M_{n}(\xi))\leq t/\sqrt{n}]\leq C_{\xi}t+2n\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{E}_{e_{1}}]+(1+O(\exp(-c_{\xi}n)))\bigg(n(n-1)\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{E}_{e_{1}+e_{2}}]+n(n-1)\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{E}_{e_{1}-e_{2}}]\bigg).

By applying Theorem 1.2 with t=0t=0 for the upper bound, and considering the probability that a row or column is zero, or that two rows or two columns are the same (up to a sign) for the lower bound (cf. the corresponding calculation in [13, Section 3.2]), we thus establish the following strengthening of Conjecture 1.1 for discrete distributions which are not uniform on their support.

Corollary 1.3.

Let ξ\xi be a discrete random variable which is not uniform on its support. There exists cξ>0c_{\xi}>0 such that

ℙ⁡[Mn​(ξ)​​i​s​s​i​n​g​u​l​a​r]=2​n​ℙ​[ℰe1]+(1+O⁡(exp⁡(−cξ​n)))​(n⁡(n−1)​ℙ​[ℰe1+e2]+n⁡(n−1)​ℙ​[ℰe1−e2]).\mathbb{P}[M_{n}(\xi)\emph{issingular}]=2n\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{E}_{e_{1}}]+(1+O(\exp(-c_{\xi}n)))\bigg(n(n-1)\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{E}_{e_{1}+e_{2}}]+n(n-1)\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{E}_{e_{1}-e_{2}}]\bigg).

In particular, for fixed p∈(0,1),p≠1/2p\in(0,1),p\neq 1/2, there exists cp>0c_{p}>0 for which

ℙ⁡[Mn​(Ber⁡(p))​​i​s​s​i​n​g​u​l​a​r]=2​n​(1−p)n+(1+O⁡(exp⁡(−cp​n)))​n​(n−1)​(p2+(1−p)2)n.\mathbb{P}[M_{n}(\operatorname{Ber}(p))\emph{issingular}]=2n(1-p)^{n}+(1+O(\exp(-c_{p}n)))n(n-1)(p^{2}+(1-p)^{2})^{n}.
Remark 0.

Let us discuss the implications of this corollary for ξ=Ber⁡(p)\xi=\operatorname{Ber}(p).

  • •

    For fixed p∈(1/2,1)p\in(1/2,1), Corollary 1.3 provides the leading term in the asymptotic expansion of the singularity probability of Mn​(Ber⁡(p))M_{n}(\operatorname{Ber}(p)). Prior to this work, even the correct value of limn→∞n−1logℙ[Mn(Ber(p)) is singular)]\lim_{n\to\infty}n^{-1}\log\mathbb{P}[M_{n}(\operatorname{Ber}(p))\text{ is singular})] had not been determined; compared to the true value of (p2+(1−p)2)(p^{2}+(1-p)^{2}) for this quantity, the previous best-known result of Bourgain, Vu, and Wood [2] provides a weaker upper bound of p\sqrt{p}. The reason that the case p∈(1/2,1)p\in(1/2,1) is more challenging than p∈(0,1/2)p\in(0,1/2) (treated in [1, 13, 4], see the discussion below) is that in the former case, the dominant contribution to the probability of singularity comes from the event of two rows or columns being equal to each other, whereas in the latter case, the dominant contribution comes from the much simpler event of a single row or column being zero.

  • •

    However, even for fixed p∈(0,1/2)p\in(0,1/2), we obtain more precise results than those in the recent work of Litvak and Tikhomirov [13] as well as [23, 7]. Namely, Corollary 1.3 provides the first two terms in the asymptotic expansion of the singularity probability of Mn​(Ber⁡(p))M_{n}(\operatorname{Ber}(p)); a result of this precision was not available before in any context.

For general discrete distributions, we determine the value of limn→∞n−1​log⁡ℙ⁡[Mn​(ξ)​ is singular]\lim_{n\to\infty}n^{-1}\log{\mathbb{P}[M_{n}(\xi)\text{ is singular}]}. The only case not covered by Theorem 1.2 is that of uniform distributions, which we handle with a non-exact main term.

Theorem 1.4.

Let ξ\xi be a discrete random variable. There exists Cξ>0C_{\xi}>0 such that for any fixed ϵ>0\epsilon>0 and for all sufficiently large nn and all t≥0t\geq 0,

ℙ[sn(Mn)≤t/n]≤Cξt+2nℙ[ℰe1]+(1+ϵ)nℙ[ℰe1−e2].\mathbb{P}[s_{n}(M_{n})\leq t/\sqrt{n}]\leq C_{\xi}t+2n\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{E}_{e_{1}}]+(1+\epsilon)^{n}\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{E}_{e_{1}-e_{2}}].
Remark 0.

For non-uniform discrete distributions, Theorem 1.2 is strictly stronger.

1.1. Previous work

Let us put Theorems 1.2 and 1.4 in the context of known results. For convenience, we will use qn​(ξ)q_{n}(\xi) to denote ℙ​[Mn​(ξ)​ is singular]\mathbb{P}[M_{n}(\xi)\text{ is singular}]. The work of Komlós [11] was the first to show that qn​(Ber⁡(1/2))=on​(1)q_{n}(\operatorname{Ber}(1/2))=o_{n}(1). Much later, an exponential bound on qn​(Ber⁡(1/2))q_{n}(\operatorname{Ber}(1/2)) was obtained by Kahn, Komlós, and Szemerédi [9]. Subsequently, the base of the exponent was improved to 0.9390.939 and 3/4+on​(1)3/4+o_{n}(1) in a series of works by Tao and Vu [21, 22], and later to 1/2+on​(1)1/\sqrt{2}+o_{n}(1) by Bourgain, Vu, and Wood [2]. Finally, a truly breakthrough result of Tikhomirov [23] in 2018 established that qn​(Ber⁡(p))=(1−p+on​(1))nq_{n}(\operatorname{Ber}(p))=(1-p+o_{n}(1))^{n} for fixed p∈(0,1/2]p\in(0,1/2]. As mentioned earlier, for fixed p∈(1/2,1)p\in(1/2,1), the analogous result was not known prior to this work.

Conjecture 1.1 has been most accessible for sparse Bernoulli distributions, in which case, the right hand side simplifies considerably to (1+on​(1))⋅2​n​ℙ​[ℰe1](1+o_{n}(1))\cdot 2n\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{E}_{e_{1}}]. Here, by the Bernoulli distribution with parameter pp, which we will henceforth denote by Ber⁡(p)\operatorname{Ber}(p), we mean the two point distribution which attains the value 11 with probability pp and the value 00 with probability 1−p1-p. Basak and Rudelson [1] confirmed the conjecture for ξ=Ber⁡(pn)\xi=\operatorname{Ber}(p_{n}) for pnp_{n} in a certain range of sparsity limited to n−1​ln⁡n−ωn​(n−1)≤pn≤n−1​ln⁡n+on​(n−1​ln⁡ln⁡n)n^{-1}\ln n-\omega_{n}(n^{-1})\leq p_{n}\leq n^{-1}\ln n+o_{n}(n^{-1}\ln\ln n). Subsequently, Litvak and Tikhomirov showed that the conjecture also holds for ξ=Ber⁡(pn)\xi=\operatorname{Ber}(p_{n}) for C​n−1​ln⁡n≤pn≤cCn^{-1}\ln n\leq p_{n}\leq c, where c>0c>0 is a small absolute constant and C>0C>0 is a large absolute constant. Recent work of Huang [4] was able to bridge the gap between the regimes covered in [1] and [4], leaving open the regime p∈(c,1/2)p\in(c,1/2). Establishing Conjecture 1.1 (as opposed to the stronger Theorem 1.2) in this regime does not require the full strength of the ideas in this paper – since this is a case of substantial interest (see Problem 8.2 in the recent work of Litvak and Tikhomirov [13]), we have provided the much simpler details in the self-contained companion note [7], which also serves as a gentle introduction to the present work and contains complete details of some relatively standard arguments which are only sketched in the present work.

For general discrete distributions ξ\xi, the only previous systematic study in the literature is the work of Bourgain, Vu, and Wood [2]. They show [2, Corollary 1.2] that if ξ\xi is a discrete distribution with supr∈ℝP[ξ=r]=:p\sup_{r\in\mathbb{R}}\operatorname{P}[\xi=r]=:p, then qn​(ξ)≤(p+on​(1))nq_{n}(\xi)\leq(\sqrt{p}+o_{n}(1))^{n}, which is far from optimal (the true bound is never more than (p+on​(1))n(p+o_{n}(1))^{n}, although it may be much smaller). On the other hand, up to a possible on​(1)o_{n}(1) term, Theorem 1.4 in this work always obtains the correct base of the exponent.

For certain specific distributions, Bourgain, Vu, and Wood obtain the correct base of the exponent (again, up to a on​(1)o_{n}(1) term). Specifically, they show [2, Corollaries 3.1, 3.2] that if ξ1,μ\xi_{1,\mu} is a random variable taking on the value 00 with probability 1−μ1-\mu and ±1\pm 1 with probability μ/2\mu/2 each, and if ξ2,μ\xi_{2,\mu} is a random variable taking on the value 00 with probability 1−μ1-\mu and ±1,±2\pm 1,\pm 2 with probability μ/4\mu/4 each, then qn​(ξ1,μ)=(1−μ+on​(1))nq_{n}(\xi_{1,\mu})=(1-\mu+o_{n}(1))^{n} for all μ∈(0,1/2)\mu\in(0,1/2) and qn​(ξ2,μ)=(1−μ+on​(1))nq_{n}(\xi_{2,\mu})=(1-\mu+o_{n}(1))^{n} for all μ∈(0,16/25)\mu\in(0,16/25). For these random variables, Theorem 1.4 determines the correct base of the singularity probability for all fixed μ∈(0,1)\mu\in(0,1), and Theorem 1.2 determines the leading order in the asymptotic expansion for μ∈(0,1),μ≠2/3\mu\in(0,1),\mu\neq 2/3 in the first case, and μ∈(0,1),μ≠4/5\mu\in(0,1),\mu\neq 4/5 in the second case. In fact, for μ∈(0,2/3)\mu\in(0,2/3) in the first case, and μ∈(0,4/5)\mu\in(0,4/5) in the second case, Theorem 1.2 determines the first two terms in the asymptotic expansion.

We remark that the results of [2] such as [2, Corollary 1.2] are also applicable to discrete random variables valued in the complex numbers, and settings where the entries of Mn​(ξ)M_{n}(\xi) are not identically distributed, and a small number of rows of Mn​(ξ)M_{n}(\xi) are possibly deterministic; we have not pursued these extensions.

Finally, we remark that there was a recent paper of Irmatov [5] which claimed to resolve Conjecture 1.1 for Rademacher random matrices. Experts have informed us that there are some unresolved issues in that work that its author is aware of, including [5, Theorem 3]. Furthermore, upon slight modification, the proof in [5] would appear to give impossibly good error terms.

1.2. Additional results

The next result addresses the main question left open by our work, namely, the resolution of Conjecture 1.1 for discrete distributions ξ\xi which are uniform on their support. In this direction, we provide a sharp analysis of the contribution of a certain low-entropy part of the unit sphere; in fact, it is this contribution which forms the leading term of the conjectured asymptotic expansion of the singularity probability. This theorem is also central to the proofs of Theorems 1.2 and 1.4.

Theorem 1.5.

Fix a discrete distribution ξ\xi. There exist δ,ρ,η>0\delta,\rho,\eta>0 depending on ξ\xi such that for all sufficiently large nn and t≤1t\leq 1,

ℙ[infx∈Cons⁡(δ,ρ)∥Mn(ξ)x∥2≤t]≤nℙ[ℰe1]+(n2)(ℙ[ℰe1−e2]+ℙ[ℰe1+e2])+(t+ℙ[ℰe1−e2])e−η​n.\mathbb{P}\bigg[\inf_{x\in\operatorname{Cons}(\delta,\rho)}\lVert M_{n}(\xi)x\rVert_{2}\leq t\bigg]\leq n\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{E}_{e_{1}}]+\binom{n}{2}(\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{E}_{e_{1}-e_{2}}]+\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{E}_{e_{1}+e_{2}}])+(t+\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{E}_{e_{1}-e_{2}}])e^{-\eta n}.

The set Cons⁡(δ,ρ)\operatorname{Cons}(\delta,\rho) appearing above is the set of unit vectors which have at least (1−δ)​n(1-\delta)n coordinates within distance ρ/n\rho/\sqrt{n} of each other (see Definition 3.1), although a trivial modification shows this result holds for any sufficiently low-entropy subset of the unit sphere.

Remark 0.

In the companion note [7], as a natural consequence of our study of anti-concentration on slices, we are able to resolve a conjecture of Nguyen [16, Conjecture 1.4] on the probability of singularity for a certain combinatorial model of random matrices. Namely, let QnQ_{n} be an n×nn\times n random matrix with independent rows, each of which is chosen uniformly from among those vectors in {0,1}n\{0,1\}^{n} which have sum exactly ⌊n/2⌋\lfloor n/2\rfloor. In [16], Nguyen showed that ℙ⁡[Qn​ is singular]=OC​(n−C)\mathbb{P}[Q_{n}\text{ is singular}]=O_{C}(n^{-C}) for any C>0C>0, and conjectured [16, Conjecture 1.4] that ℙ⁡[Qn​ is singular]=(1/2+on​(1))n\mathbb{P}[Q_{n}\text{ is singular}]=(1/2+o_{n}(1))^{n}. After intermediate work [3, 6], an exponential upper bound on the singularity probability was only very recently obtained in work of Tran [24], the key difficulty being establishing even relatively coarse inverse Littlewood–Offord type results for the slice. In [7], we settle [16, Conjecture 1.4] using the techniques developed in this work.

Theorem 1.6 ([7, Theorem 1.4]).

For every ϵ>0\epsilon>0, there exists CϵC_{\epsilon} depending on ϵ\epsilon such that for all sufficiently large nn, and for all t≥0t\geq 0,

ℙ[sn(Qn)≤t/n]≤Cϵt+(1/2+ϵ)n.\mathbb{P}[s_{n}(Q_{n})\leq t/\sqrt{n}]\leq C_{\epsilon}t+(1/2+\epsilon)^{n}.

1.3. Overview of the techniques

As in many works in this area, we use the high-level strategy (going back to Kašin [10] and subsequently used in [20, 12, 19, 18]) of dividing the unit sphere into ‘structured’ and ‘unstructured’ components, and estimating the contribution of each part separately. However, compared to previous works, the treatment of both components require overcoming significant obstacles which unavoidably arise in the sharp analysis of the invertibility of random matrices in any amount of generality.

For instance, in the analysis of structured vectors, we need to additionally capture the event that two rows/columns of the matrix are equal (up to a sign) whereas previous considerations of sharp invertibility only addressed scenarios where the dominant contribution to the probability of singularity is due to a single row or column being zero. As discussed in the remark after Corollary 1.3, this is a fundamental issue. Moreover, in the analysis of unstructured vectors, we need precise metric entropy estimates for the anti-concentration problem with respect to random vectors on general multi-slices. Obtaining partial estimates of this nature (which are not sufficient to prove Conjecture 1.1) even for the special case of the Boolean slice is already a highly non-trivial endeavor which is at the heart of the recent work of Litvak and Tikhomirov [13], where it is accomplished using the substantially more involved notion of the ‘UDLCD’.

Structured vectors: The structured vectors in our work are ‘almost-constant vectors’ i.e. those vectors on 𝕊n−1\mathbb{S}^{n-1} which have (1−δ)​n(1-\delta)n coordinates within distance ρ/n\rho/\sqrt{n} of each other, where δ,ρ>0\delta,\rho>0 are sufficiently small constants. This class of structured vectors arises naturally in the consideration of the anti-concentration property of a sequence of numbers with respect to a random vector constrained to lie in a ‘slice’. Moreover, since vectors which are close to the standard basis vectors eie_{i} or to ei±eje_{i}\pm e_{j} clearly play a special role in the problem under consideration, it is natural to separately handle ‘elementary’ and ‘non-elementary’ structured vectors.

Our treatment of structured vectors, culminating in Theorem 1.5, requires significant innovations compared to previous works on the sharp invertibility of sparse random Bernoulli matrices [1, 13, 4] – in the sparse Bernoulli case, the corresponding class of elementary vectors only needs to consist of those vectors which are close to some eie_{i}, and the largest atom of the the random variable Ber⁡(p)\operatorname{Ber}(p) is conveniently at 00. We refer the reader to [7] for the much simpler argument in this case.

In the present work, in order to handle non-elementary vectors, we need to develop novel sharp anticoncentration estimates Propositions 5.2 and 5.3 (in contrast, the essentially standard estimate [7, Lemma 2.6] was sufficient for the corresponding step in [7]). Even more involved is the analysis of elementary vectors, for which we develop a new technique. Let us begin by discussing this technique for ξ=Ber⁡(p)\xi=\operatorname{Ber}(p) for fixed p∈(0,1/2)p\in(0,1/2), in which case, the elementary vectors are those which are close to some standard basis vector. For concreteness, consider vectors which are sufficiently close to e1e_{1}. We show that, if any such vector has exponentially small image, then either the first column of the matrix is the zero vector, or it must belong to a universal subset of nonzero vectors of {0,1}n\{0,1\}^{n} of measure at most (1−p+ϵ)n(1-p+\epsilon)^{n}. The first case corresponds to the term ℙ⁡[ℰe1]\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{E}_{e_{1}}] in Conjecture 1.1; for the second case, we leverage the seminal work of Rudelson and Vershynin to show that, on our event, the probability that any vector in this universal subset appears as the first column of the matrix is at most exp⁡(−4​ϵ​n)\exp(-4\epsilon n), at which point we can conclude using the union bound.

Of course, for general discrete random variables ξ\xi, one must enlarge the class of elementary vectors to include unit vectors which are close to (ei±ej)/2(e_{i}\pm e_{j})/\sqrt{2} and unit vectors which are close to eie_{i}. In the first case (Propositions 5.5 and 5.7), we use a rotation trick to reduce to a situation where we can use an analysis similar to (but more complicated than) the one outlined in the previous paragraph. The second case requires a very careful treatment since we are aiming for a leading term of the form (ℙ[ξ=0])n(\mathbb{P}[\xi=0])^{n} (as opposed to (supr∈ℝℙ[ξ=r])n(\sup_{r\in\mathbb{R}}\mathbb{P}[\xi=r])^{n}), and moreover, the desired error is (ℙ[ξ=ξ′]−η)n(\mathbb{P}[\xi=\xi^{\prime}]-\eta)^{n} which may be very small. To accomplish this, we first prove a version of Theorem 1.4 with an estimate on the singularity probability of the form (supr∈ℝℙ[ξ=r]+on(1))n(\sup_{r\in\mathbb{R}}\mathbb{P}[\xi=r]+o_{n}(1))^{n} (Propositions 4.4 and 4.5), and then leverage these preliminary estimates to obtain the desired bound.

We emphasize that our treatment of structured vectors, as captured by Theorem 1.5, is not sensitive to the non-uniformity of the distribution ξ\xi. In particular, given Theorems 1.2 and 1.5, the only missing case in the complete resolution of Conjecture 1.1 (in fact, in a stronger form) is a sharp analysis of unstructured vectors in the case when ξ\xi is uniform on its support.

Unstructured vectors: The unstructured vectors are the complement of the structured vectors i.e.  those which do not have a (1−δ)(1-\delta)-fraction of their coordinates within ρ/n\rho/\sqrt{n} of each other. Our treatment of these vectors relies on the non-uniformity of ξ\xi by exploiting the gap between ℙ[ξ=ξ′]\mathbb{P}[\xi=\xi^{\prime}] and the entropy of ξ\xi; the idea to exploit such a gap to prove sharp invertibility results (in the case of Bernoulli random variables) is due to Litvak and Tikhomirov [13].

The main ingredient in our work for handling such vectors is Theorem 2.1, which is an extension of [23, Theorem B] to a (real) multislice, i.e., the set of vectors in {a1,…,ak}n\{a_{1},\dots,a_{k}\}^{n} which have a prescribed number of coordinates taking on each of the values a1,…,aka_{1},\dots,a_{k}. Such a result was previously not known even for the Boolean slice; indeed, the work [13] uses a rather involved notion of arithmetic structure to study anti-concentration on Boolean slices, which is not powerful enough to handle slices that are not very far from the central slice. We remark that in general, even establishing much less precise versions of [23, Theorem B] on the Boolean slice has been very challenging, despite much work due to the natural connection to certain combinatorial models of random matrices (cf. [8] and the references therein).

Compared to [23, Theorem B], we need to overcome two challenges. The first, as mentioned above, is the lack of independence between the coordinates of a vector uniformly distributed on the multi-slice. The second challenge is that a1,…,aka_{1},\dots,a_{k} are now arbitrary real numbers (corresponding to the support of ξ\xi), and hence, certain arguments tailored for integers no longer apply. Overcoming these challenges requires additional ideas, which we discuss in Section 2. The reader is also referred to [7, Theorem 3.1] where we record the proof for the Boolean slice, a setting which encounters the first challenge but not the second.

1.4. Notation

For a positive integer NN, 𝕊N−1\mathbb{S}^{N-1} denotes the set of unit vectors in ℝN\mathbb{R}^{N}, and if x∈ℝNx\in\mathbb{R}^{N} and r≥0r\geq 0 then 𝔹2N​(x,r)\mathbb{B}_{2}^{N}(x,r) denotes the radius rr Euclidean ball in ℝN\mathbb{R}^{N} centered at xx. ∥⋅∥2\lVert\cdot\rVert_{2} denotes the standard Euclidean norm of a vector, and for a matrix A=(ai​j)A=(a_{ij}), ∥A∥\lVert A\rVert is its spectral norm (i.e., ℓ2→ℓ2\ell^{2}\to\ell^{2} operator norm).

We will let [N][N] denote the interval {1,…,N}\{1,\dots,N\}. For nonnegative integers m≤nm\leq n, we let {0,1}mn\{0,1\}^{n}_{m} be the set of vectors in {0,1}n\{0,1\}^{n} with sum mm.

Since it is essential throughout the paper, we formally record the definition of a discrete random variable and the corresponding random matrix.

Definition 1.7.

We say that a random variable ξ\xi is a discrete random variable (equivalently, has a discrete distribution) if it is real-valued, its support is finite, and the support contains at least two distinct points. Mn​(ξ)M_{n}(\xi) denotes the n×nn\times n random matrix, with independent entries that are copies of ξ\xi.

For ξ\xi a discrete random variable with k=|supp⁡(ξ)|k=|\operatorname{supp}(\xi)| (so that k≥2k\geq 2), we will denote its support by a→=(a1,…,ak)\vec{a}=(a_{1},\dots,a_{k}), and the (nonzero) probabilities of attaining a1,…,aka_{1},\dots,a_{k} by p→=(p1,…,pk)\vec{p}=(p_{1},\dots,p_{k}). Note that ∥p→∥1=1\lVert\vec{p}\rVert_{1}=1, and ∥p→∥22≤∥p→∥∞\lVert\vec{p}\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq\lVert\vec{p}\rVert_{\infty} with equality if and only if ξ\xi is uniform on its support. We will use H⁡(ξ)H(\xi) to denote the natural-logarithmic entropy of ξ\xi, i.e., H(ξ)=H(p→)=∑i=1k−pilog(pi)H(\xi)=H(\vec{p})=\sum_{i=1}^{k}-p_{i}\log(p_{i}). We will (somewhat abusively) use p0p_{0} to denote ℙ[ξ=0]\mathbb{P}[\xi=0].

For a random variable ξ\xi and a real number r≥0r\geq 0, we let ℒ(ξ,r):=supz∈ℝℙ[|ξ−z|≤r]\mathcal{L}(\xi,r):=\sup_{z\in\mathbb{R}}\mathbb{P}[|\xi-z|\leq r]. We will use ℓ1​(ℤ)\ell_{1}(\mathbb{Z}) to denote the set of functions f:ℤ→ℝf\colon\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{R} for which ∑z∈ℤ|f⁡(z)|<∞\sum_{z\in\mathbb{Z}}|f(z)|<\infty.

We will also make use of asymptotic notation. For functions f,gf,g, f=Oα​(g)f=O_{\alpha}(g) (or f≲αgf\lesssim_{\alpha}g) means that f≤Cα​gf\leq C_{\alpha}g, where CαC_{\alpha} is some constant depending on α\alpha; f=Ωα​(g)f=\Omega_{\alpha}(g) (or f≳αgf\gtrsim_{\alpha}g) means that f≥cα​gf\geq c_{\alpha}g, where cα>0c_{\alpha}>0 is some constant depending on α\alpha, and f=Θα​(g)f=\Theta_{\alpha}(g) means that both f=Oα​(g)f=O_{\alpha}(g) and f=Ωα​(g)f=\Omega_{\alpha}(g) hold. For parameters ϵ,δ\epsilon,\delta, we write ϵ≪δ\epsilon\ll\delta to mean that ϵ≤c⁡(δ)\epsilon\leq c(\delta) for a sufficient function cc.

Finally, we will omit floors and ceilings where they make no essential difference.

1.5. Organization

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we prove our key inversion of randomness estimate for conditional thresholds on the multislice, Theorem 2.1. In Section 3, we use this to prove the invertibility estimate for unstructured vectors (Theorem 3.8). In the short Section 4, we prove a weaker version of Theorem 1.4; this is used in our treatment of structured vectors (i.e., the proof of Theorem 1.5), which is the content of Section 5. In Section 6, we quickly combine Theorems 1.5 and 3.8 to prove Theorems 1.2 and 1.4.

2. Inversion of randomness on the multislice

In this section, we prove our key inversion of randomness result, Theorem 2.1. We will focus on the non-independent “multislice” version as its deduction is strictly harder than the independent version, Theorem 2.14 (which we will only use to establish the preliminary estimate Theorem 4.5).

The proof of Theorem 2.1 follows a direction introduced by Tikhomirov [23]. In this approach, the relevant Lévy concentration function of a random vector is replaced with certain random averages of functions. One then shows that the random vectors with large values of the Lévy concentration function are super-exponentially rare, by first demonstrating a weaker notion of anticoncentration after revealing (1−ϵ)​n(1-\epsilon)n coordinates of the random vector, and then iterating a smoothing procedure on linear-sized pieces of the vector which allows one to bootstrap the strength of anticoncentration considered.

Our major challenges lie in (i) the non-independence of the coordinates of a vector on the multislice, as the arguments in [23] rely strongly on the independence structure of the considered model, and (ii) the freedom to allow the support of ξ\xi to consist of arbitrary real numbers, as certain arguments in [23] rely on the integrality of the support.

The reader may benefit from first perusing a simpler version of this argument, for slices of the Boolean hypercube, which is presented in the companion note [7, Section 3]. We will often note the corresponding statements in [7] for the reader’s convenience.

2.1. Statement and preliminaries

Let N,n≥1N,n\geq 1 be integers and let 0<δ<1/40<\delta<1/4, K3>K2>K1>1K_{3}>K_{2}>K_{1}>1 be real parameters. We say that 𝒜⊆ℤn\mathcal{A}\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^{n} is (N,n,K1,K2,K3,δ)(N,n,K_{1},K_{2},K_{3},\delta)-admissible if

    maxi⁡max⁡{|a|:a∈Ai}≤n​N\max_{i}\max\{|a|:a\in A_{i}\}\leq nN,

Recall at this point that ξ\xi, which has (nonzero) probabilities p→=(p1,…,pk)\vec{p}=(p_{1},\ldots,p_{k}) on atoms a→=(a1,…,ak)\vec{a}=(a_{1},\ldots,a_{k}), is fixed. For any f:ℝ→ℝf:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}, any 0≤ℓ≤n0\leq\ell\leq n, and any s→∈ℤ≥0k\vec{s}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{k} with ∥s→∥1=ℓ\lVert\vec{s}\rVert_{1}=\ell, define the random function (depending on the randomness of X1,…,XnX_{1},\dots,X_{n}):

f𝒜,s→,ℓ(t):=𝔼b[f(t+∑i=1ℓbiXi)|#{bi=aj}=sj∀j∈[k]],f_{\mathcal{A},\vec{s},\ell}(t):=\mathbb{E}_{b}\bigg[f\bigg(t+\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}b_{i}X_{i}\bigg)\bigg|\#\{b_{i}=a_{j}\}=s_{j}\forall j\in[k]\bigg],

where 𝔼b\mathbb{E}_{b} denotes the expectation over a random vector b=(b1,…,bℓ)∈ℝℓb=(b_{1},\dots,b_{\ell})\in\mathbb{R}^{\ell} with coordinates independently distributed as ξ\xi. The conditioning encodes that for all j∈[k]j\in[k], there are exactly sjs_{j} coordinates (out of ℓ\ell) where bb hits the atom aja_{j}.

Proof sketch.

This is essentially the same as the deduction in [23, Corollary 4.3]. We apply Theorem 2.1 to f(t):=2−|t|/n/ιf(t):=2^{-|t|/\sqrt{n}}/\iota, where t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R} and ι\iota is an appropriate normalization, separately for all m→∈ℤ≥0k\vec{m}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{k} such that ∥m→−p→​n∥∞≤γ2.1​n\lVert\vec{m}-\vec{p}n\rVert_{\infty}\leq\gamma_{\ref{thm:inversion-of-randomness}}n, and then conclude using a union bound. ∎

The proof of Theorem 2.1 makes use of an anticoncentration estimate on the multislice, which we record below (Lemmas 2.5 and 2.6), and is ultimately a consequence of the following standard anticoncentration inequality due to Kolmogorov-Lévy-Rogozin.

Lemma 2.4 ([17]).

Let ξ1,…,ξn\xi_{1},\dots,\xi_{n} be independent random variables. Then, for any real numbers r1,…,rn>0r_{1},\dots,r_{n}>0 and any real r≥maxi∈[n]⁡rir\geq\max_{i\in[n]}r_{i}, we have

ℒ⁡(∑i=1nξi,r)≤C2.4​r∑i=1n(1−ℒ⁡(ξi,ri))​ri2,\displaystyle\mathcal{L}\bigg(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\xi_{i},r\bigg)\leq\frac{C_{\ref{lem:LKR}}r}{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(1-\mathcal{L}(\xi_{i},r_{i}))r_{i}^{2}}},

where C2.4>0C_{\ref{lem:LKR}}>0 is an absolute constant.

Lemma 2.5.

Fix (a1,…,ak)∈ℝk(a_{1},\ldots,a_{k})\in\mathbb{R}^{k} with distinct coordinates. Let σ,λ∈(0,1/3)\sigma,\lambda\in(0,1/3) and r>0r>0. ℒ⁡(∑i=1nzi​bi,r⋅mini<j⁡|ai−aj|)≤C2.5n,\mathcal{L}\bigg(\sum_{i=1}^{n}z_{i}b_{i},r\cdot\min_{i<j}|a_{i}-a_{j}|\bigg)\leq\frac{C_{\ref{lem:mslkr}}}{\sqrt{n}},

We will now use the randomness within the atoms aℓa_{\ell} and aℓ′a_{\ell^{\prime}} in order to derive the anticoncentration result. (2.1) ℙ[|{j∈[σn]:{b2​j−1,b2​j}={aℓ,aℓ′}|≤c(σ,λ,k)n]≤exp(−c(σ,λ,k)n),\displaystyle\mathbb{P}[|\{j\in[\sigma n]:\{b_{2j-1},b_{2j}\}=\{a_{\ell},a_{\ell^{\prime}}\}|\leq c(\sigma,\lambda,k)n]\leq\exp(-c(\sigma,\lambda,k)n),

2.2. Preprocessing on real-valued multislices

As in [23], we first prove a version of Theorem 2.1 in which LL is allowed to depend on MM.

Proposition 2.7.

Fix a discrete distribution ξ\xi. For 0<δ<1/40<\delta<1/4, K3>K2>K1>1K_{3}>K_{2}>K_{1}>1, ϵ≪min⁡(p→)\epsilon\ll\min(\vec{p}), and a given parameter M≥1M\geq 1, there is γ2.7=γ2.7​(ξ,ϵ,δ,K1,K2,K3)∈(0,ϵ)\gamma_{\ref{prop:rough-Linfty}}=\gamma_{\ref{prop:rough-Linfty}}(\xi,\epsilon,\delta,K_{1},K_{2},K_{3})\in(0,\epsilon) independent of MM and there are L2.7=L2.7​(ξ,ϵ,δ,K1,K2,K3,M)>0L_{\ref{prop:rough-Linfty}}=L_{\ref{prop:rough-Linfty}}(\xi,\epsilon,\delta,K_{1},K_{2},K_{3},M)>0 and n2.7=n2.7​(ξ,ϵ,δ,K1,K2,K3,M)≥1n_{\ref{prop:rough-Linfty}}=n_{\ref{prop:rough-Linfty}}(\xi,\epsilon,\delta,K_{1},K_{2},K_{3},M)\geq 1 such that the following holds.

Let n≥n2.7n\geq n_{\ref{prop:rough-Linfty}}, 1≤N≤exp⁡((H⁡(p→)−ϵ)​n)1\leq N\leq\exp((H(\vec{p})-\epsilon)n), and 𝒜\mathcal{A} be (N,n,K1,K2,K3,δ)(N,n,K_{1},K_{2},K_{3},\delta)-admissible. Let ff be a nonnegative function in L1​(ℝ)L^{1}(\mathbb{R}) with ∥f∥1=1\lVert f\rVert_{1}=1 such that log2⁡f\log_{2}{f} is 11-Lipschitz. Then, for all ℓ∈[(1−γ2.7)​n,n]\ell\in[(1-\gamma_{\ref{prop:rough-Linfty}})n,n] and s→∈ℤ≥0k\vec{s}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{k} with ∥s→∥1=ℓ\lVert\vec{s}\rVert_{1}=\ell and ∥s→−p→​ℓ∥∞≤γ2.7​ℓ\lVert\vec{s}-\vec{p}\ell\rVert_{\infty}\leq\gamma_{\ref{prop:rough-Linfty}}\ell, we have

ℙ[∥f𝒜,s→,ℓ∥∞≥L2.7(Nn)−1]≤exp(−Mn).\mathbb{P}\bigg[\lVert f_{\mathcal{A},\vec{s},\ell}\rVert_{\infty}\geq L_{\ref{prop:rough-Linfty}}(N\sqrt{n})^{-1}\bigg]\leq\exp(-Mn).

For a simpler version of this argument, we refer the reader to the proof of [7, Proposition 3.6]. Proposition 2.7 should be seen as an analogue of [23, Lemma 4.6] for the multislice. As mentioned earlier, compared to [23], our situation is much more delicate since we are working with a vector with non-independent coordinates and need to extract a term corresponding to the entropy of the multislice. Such complications are already encountered when working with a Boolean slice, as in [7, Proposition 3.6]. Working on real multislices presents additional difficulties (along with significant notational complications), owing to the fact that we are working on L1​(ℝ)L^{1}(\mathbb{R}); this extension is handled by using the log-Lipschitz condition on ff. We note that the corresponding statements in [7, 23] do not need to use any log-Lipschitz assumption at this stage of the argument since they are proved for ℓ1​(ℤ)\ell^{1}(\mathbb{Z}). We also note that, while the constant 11 in 11-log-Lipschitz is arbitrary, some condition of this nature is necessary to rule out ff being very close to a Dirac mass ([23]).

We first note the trivial recursive relation

f𝒜,s→,ℓ​(t)=∑i=1ksiℓ​f𝒜,s→−ei,ℓ−1​(t+ai​Xℓ)f_{\mathcal{A},\vec{s},\ell}(t)=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\frac{s_{i}}{\ell}f_{\mathcal{A},\vec{s}-e_{i},\ell-1}(t+a_{i}X_{\ell})

for all 1≤ℓ≤n1\leq\ell\leq n and s→∈ℤ≥0k\vec{s}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{k} with ∥s→∥1=ℓ\lVert\vec{s}\rVert_{1}=\ell. If any coordinate of s→\vec{s} is zero, note the corresponding term (which would be undefined) has a coefficient of 00, and drops out. Note also that, by definition, f𝒜,0→,0=ff_{\mathcal{A},\vec{0},0}=f.

We are now ready to prove Proposition 2.7.

2.3. Refining the initial estimate

We now need to remove the dependence of LL on MM. This is accomplished by the main result of this subsection, Proposition 2.11, which is a multislice and L1​(ℝ)L^{1}(\mathbb{R}) analogue of [23, Proposition 4.10]. Even though we are working in the much more complicated setting of real multislices, remarkably, our proof of Proposition 2.11 is able to use [23, Proposition 4.10] as a black box: roughly, we first use a re-randomization procedure to reduce smoothing on the multislice for L1​(ℝ)L^{1}(\mathbb{R}) to smoothing on the hypercube, also for L1​(ℝ)L^{1}(\mathbb{R}). At this juncture, the necessary smoothing estimate on the hypercube for L1​(ℝ)L^{1}(\mathbb{R}) can in fact be lifted from the smoothing estimate for the hypercube for ℓ1​(ℤ)\ell^{1}(\mathbb{Z}), proved in [23]. In particular, we reduce the smoothing estimate for general log-Lipschitz functions in L1​(ℝ)L^{1}(\mathbb{R}) to that of a simpler class of “step” functions, which in turn is equivalent to ℓ1​(ℤ)\ell^{1}(\mathbb{Z}).

A simpler version of this argument, for Boolean slices, is presented in [7, Proposition 3.10].

2.4. Deriving the final result

Theorem 2.1 is almost immediate given the previous propositions.

Proof of Theorem 2.1.

The proof of Theorem 2.1 given Propositions 2.7 and 2.11 is similar to the derivation in [23, Theorem 4.2]; we refer the reader to the companion note [7, Theorem 3.1] for a leisurely account of the complete details. In words, we use Proposition 2.7 to show that any revelation of the first (1−γ)​n(1-\gamma)n random variables (for suitably chosen γ\gamma) will give an L∞L^{\infty} bound at roughly the right scale L′​(N​n)−1L^{\prime}(N\sqrt{n})^{-1}, where L′L^{\prime} depends on MM. Then, we divide the remaining random variables into a constant number of pieces (this number depends on L′L^{\prime} and C2.5C_{\ref{lem:mslkr}} with appropriate parameters), and use Proposition 2.11 iteratively on these pieces. As in Steps 2 and 3 in the proof of [7, Theorem 3.1], we may restrict our attention to the case when each of the remaining pieces is a well-conditioned multislice (this automatically implies that the first (1−γ)​n(1-\gamma)n coordinates are also a well-conditioned multislice), noting that the complement of this event occurs with very low probability, and the product of this probability with L′​(N​n)−1L^{\prime}(N\sqrt{n})^{-1} is much smaller than the bound on the essential sup-norm that we are aiming for. ∎

2.5. Independent model

We conclude this section with an analogue of Corollary 2.3 in the independent case.

Theorem 2.14.

Fix a discrete distribution ξ\xi. For 0<δ<1/40<\delta<1/4, K3>K2>K1>1K_{3}>K_{2}>K_{1}>1, ϵ≪∥p→∥∞\epsilon\ll\lVert\vec{p}\rVert_{\infty}, and a given parameter M≥1M\geq 1, there is L2.14=L2.14​(ξ,ϵ,δ,K1,K2,K3)>0L_{\ref{cor:independent-threshold-inversion}}=L_{\ref{cor:independent-threshold-inversion}}(\xi,\epsilon,\delta,K_{1},K_{2},K_{3})>0 independent of MM and n2.14=n2.14​(ξ,ϵ,δ,K1,K2,K3,M)≥1n_{\ref{cor:independent-threshold-inversion}}=n_{\ref{cor:independent-threshold-inversion}}(\xi,\epsilon,\delta,K_{1},K_{2},K_{3},M)\geq 1 such that the following holds.

Let n≥n2.14n\geq n_{\ref{cor:independent-threshold-inversion}}, 1≤N≤∥p→∥∞−n​exp⁡(−ϵ​n)1\leq N\leq\lVert\vec{p}\rVert_{\infty}^{-n}\exp(-\epsilon n) and 𝒜\mathcal{A} be (N,n,K1,K2,K3,δ)(N,n,K_{1},K_{2},K_{3},\delta)-admissible. Then

|{x∈𝒜:ℒξ​(∑i=1nbi​xi,n)≥L2.14​N−1}|≤e−M​n​|𝒜|.\bigg|\bigg\{x\in\mathcal{A}:\mathcal{L}_{\xi}\bigg(\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_{i}x_{i},\sqrt{n}\bigg)\geq L_{\ref{cor:independent-threshold-inversion}}N^{-1}\bigg\}\bigg|\leq e^{-Mn}|\mathcal{A}|.

The proof of Theorem 2.14 is analogous to that of Theorem 2.1 followed by Corollary 2.3, except that the random variables bib_{i} are now independent copies of ξ\xi. This independence simplifies matters dramatically, as one can derive an analogue of Proposition 2.7 by simply considering drops (as in [23, Proposition 4.5]) instead of “well-conditioned” drops, and then using subsampling arguments similar to those appearing above to prove analogues of Proposition 2.11 and Theorem 2.1. We leave the details to the interested reader.

3. Non-almost-constant vectors

3.1. Preliminaries

We recall the following basic definition of almost-constant vectors.

Definition 3.1.

We define Cons⁡(δ,ρ)\operatorname{Cons}(\delta,\rho) to be the set of x∈𝕊n−1x\in\mathbb{S}^{n-1} such that there is λ∈ℝ\lambda\in\mathbb{R} so that |xi−λ|≤ρ/n|x_{i}-\lambda|\leq\rho/\sqrt{n} for at least (1−δ)​n(1-\delta)n values i∈[n]i\in[n]. We let Noncons⁡(δ,ρ)=𝕊n−1∖Cons⁡(δ,ρ)\operatorname{Noncons}(\delta,\rho)=\mathbb{S}^{n-1}\setminus\operatorname{Cons}(\delta,\rho).

The following is a standard fact regarding non-almost-constant vectors. For the reader’s convenience, we provide complete details of the proof in [7].

Lemma 3.2 ([7, Lemma 2.3]).

For δ,ρ∈(0,1/4)\delta,\rho\in(0,1/4), there exist ν,ν′>0\nu,\nu^{\prime}>0 depending only on δ,ρ\delta,\rho, and a finite set 𝒦\mathcal{K} of positive real numbers, also depending only only on δ,ρ\delta,\rho, such that the following holds.

If x∈Noncons⁡(δ,ρ)x\in\operatorname{Noncons}(\delta,\rho), then at least one of the following two conclusions is satisfied.

  1. (1)

    There exist κ,κ′∈𝒦\kappa,\kappa^{\prime}\in\mathcal{K} such that

    |xi|≤κn​ for at least ​ν​n​ indices ​i∈[n], and |x_{i}|\leq\frac{\kappa}{\sqrt{n}}\text{ for at least }\nu n\text{ indices }i\in[n],\text{ and }
    κ+ν′n<|xi|≤κ′n​ for at least ​ν​n​ indices ​i∈[n].\frac{\kappa+\nu^{\prime}}{\sqrt{n}}<|x_{i}|\leq\frac{\kappa^{\prime}}{\sqrt{n}}\text{ for at least }\nu n\text{ indices }i\in[n].
  2. (2)

    There exist κ,κ′∈𝒦\kappa,\kappa^{\prime}\in\mathcal{K} such that

    κn<xi<κ′n​ for at least ​ν​n​ indices ​i∈[n], and \frac{\kappa}{\sqrt{n}}<x_{i}<\frac{\kappa^{\prime}}{\sqrt{n}}\text{ for at least }\nu n\text{ indices }i\in[n],\text{ and }
    −κ′n<xi<−κn​ for at least ​ν​n​ indices ​i∈[n].-\frac{\kappa^{\prime}}{\sqrt{n}}<x_{i}<-\frac{\kappa}{\sqrt{n}}\text{ for at least }\nu n\text{ indices }i\in[n].

We record two useful tensorization statements.

Lemma 3.3 ([23, Lemma 3.2]).

Let χ1,…,χm\chi_{1},\ldots,\chi_{m} be independent random variables.

  • •

    Assume that for all ϵ≥ϵ0\epsilon\geq\epsilon_{0},

    ℙ[|χi|≤ϵ]≤Kϵ.\mathbb{P}[|\chi_{i}|\leq\epsilon]\leq K\epsilon.

    Then for ϵ≥ϵ0\epsilon\geq\epsilon_{0}

    ℙ[∥(χ1,…,χm)∥2≤ϵm]≤(CKϵ)m,\mathbb{P}[\lVert(\chi_{1},\ldots,\chi_{m})\rVert_{2}\leq\epsilon\sqrt{m}]\leq(CK\epsilon)^{m},

    where CC is an absolute constant.

  • •

    Assume that for some η,τ>0\eta,\tau>0,

    ℙ[|χi|≤η]≤τ.\mathbb{P}[|\chi_{i}|\leq\eta]\leq\tau.

    Then for ϵ∈(0,1]\epsilon\in(0,1],

    ℙ[∥(χ1,…,χm)∥2≤ηϵ​m]≤(e/ϵ)ϵ​mτm−ϵ​m.\mathbb{P}[\lVert(\chi_{1},\ldots,\chi_{m})\rVert_{2}\leq\eta\sqrt{\epsilon m}]\leq(e/\epsilon)^{\epsilon m}\tau^{m-\epsilon m}.

We will need a standard concentration estimate for the operator norm of a random matrix with independent centered sub-Gaussian entries.

Lemma 3.4 ([25, Lemma 4.4.5]).

There exists an absolute constant C>0C>0 such that the following holds. Let AA be an m×nm\times n i.i.d. matrix with mean 00, sub-Gaussian entries with sub-Gaussian norm at most KK. Then for any t≥0t\geq 0 we have

ℙ[∥A∥≤C(m+n+t)]≤2exp(−t2/K2).\mathbb{P}[\lVert A\rVert\leq C(\sqrt{m}+\sqrt{n}+t)]\leq 2\exp(-t^{2}/K^{2}).

Finally, we will need the following lemma, proved using randomized rounding (cf. [14]), which is a straightforward generalization of [23, Lemma 5.3]. We omit details since the proof is identical.

Lemma 3.5.

Let y=(y1,…,yn)∈ℝny=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{n})\in\mathbb{R}^{n} be a vector, and let μ>0\mu>0, λ∈ℝ\lambda\in\mathbb{R} be fixed. Let Δ\Delta denote a probability distribution which is supported in [−s,s]n[-s,s]^{n}. There exist constants c3.5c_{\ref{lem:round}} and C3.5C_{\ref{lem:round}}, depending only on ss, for which the following holds. Suppose that for all t≥nt\geq\sqrt{n},

ℙ[|∑i=1nbiyi−λ|≤t]≤μt,\mathbb{P}\bigg[\bigg|\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_{i}y_{i}-\lambda\bigg|\leq t\bigg]\leq\mu t,

where (b1,…,bn)(b_{1},\dots,b_{n}) is distributed according to Δ\Delta. Then, there exists a vector y′=(y1′,…,yn′)∈ℤny^{\prime}=(y^{\prime}_{1},\dots,y^{\prime}_{n})\in\mathbb{Z}^{n} satisfying

  1. (R1)

    ∥y−y′∥∞≤1\lVert y-y^{\prime}\rVert_{\infty}\leq 1,

  2. (R2)

    ℙ[|∑i=1nbiyi′−λ|≤t]≤C3.5μt\mathbb{P}[|\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_{i}y_{i}^{\prime}-\lambda|\leq t]\leq C_{\ref{lem:round}}\mu t for all t≥nt\geq\sqrt{n},

  3. (R3)

    ℒ⁡(∑i=1nbi​yi′,n)≥c3.5​ℒ​(∑i=1nbi​yi,n)\mathcal{L}(\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_{i}y_{i}^{\prime},\sqrt{n})\geq c_{\ref{lem:round}}\mathcal{L}(\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_{i}y_{i},\sqrt{n}),

  4. (R4)

    |∑i=1nyi−∑i=1nyi′|≤C3.5​n|\sum_{i=1}^{n}y_{i}-\sum_{i=1}^{n}y_{i}^{\prime}|\leq C_{\ref{lem:round}}\sqrt{n}.

3.2. The structure theorem

Let ξ\xi be a discrete distribution, and let A=A⁡(ξ)A=A(\xi) denote an (n−1)×n(n-1)\times n random matrix, each of whose entries is an independent copy of a ξ\xi random variable. We fix a function v⁡(A)v(A) which takes as input an (n−1)×n(n-1)\times n matrix and outputs a unit vector in its right kernel. A key ingredient in the proof of the main result of this section, Theorem 3.8, is a structure theorem for kernel vectors of AA, which encodes the fact that (with very high probability) non-almost-constant kernel vectors of AA must be maximally unstructured in the relevant sense.

Definition 3.6.

Fix a discrete distribution ξ\xi. Let γ→∈ℝ≥0k\vec{\gamma}\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{k} with ∥γ→∥∞<min⁡(p→)\lVert\vec{\gamma}\rVert_{\infty}<\min(\vec{p}), and let L≥1L\geq 1. Then, for any integer n≥1n\geq 1 and x∈𝕊n−1x\in\mathbb{S}^{n-1}, we define

𝒯ξ,γ→​(x,L):=sup{t∈(0,1):ℒξ,γ→​(∑i=1nbi​xi,t)>L​t}.\mathcal{T}_{\xi,\vec{\gamma}}(x,L):=\sup\bigg\{t\in(0,1):\mathcal{L}_{\xi,\vec{\gamma}}\bigg(\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_{i}x_{i},t\bigg)>Lt\bigg\}.

We also define

𝒯ξ​(x,L):=sup{t∈(0,1):ℒξ​(∑i=1nbi​xi,t)>L​t}.\mathcal{T}_{\xi}(x,L):=\sup\bigg\{t\in(0,1):\mathcal{L}_{\xi}\bigg(\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_{i}x_{i},t\bigg)>Lt\bigg\}.
Proposition 3.7.

Let δ,ρ,ϵ∈(0,1)\delta,\rho,\epsilon\in(0,1). There exist L3.7=L3.7​(δ,ρ,ξ,ϵ)L_{\ref{prop:structure}}=L_{\ref{prop:structure}}(\delta,\rho,\xi,\epsilon), γ3.7=γ3.7​(δ,ρ,ξ,ϵ)\gamma_{\ref{prop:structure}}=\gamma_{\ref{prop:structure}}(\delta,\rho,\xi,\epsilon) and n3.7=n3.7​(δ,ρ,ξ,ϵ)n_{\ref{prop:structure}}=n_{\ref{prop:structure}}(\delta,\rho,\xi,\epsilon) such that for all n≥n3.7n\geq n_{\ref{prop:structure}}, with probability at least 1−k−2​n1-k^{-2n}, exactly one of the following holds.

  • •

    v⁡(A)∈Cons⁡(δ,ρ)v(A)\in\operatorname{Cons}(\delta,\rho), or

  • •

    𝒯ξ,γ3.7​1k​(v⁡(A),L3.7)≤exp⁡((ϵ−H⁡(p→))​n)\mathcal{T}_{\xi,\gamma_{\ref{prop:structure}}1_{k}}(v(A),L_{\ref{prop:structure}})\leq\exp((\epsilon-H(\vec{p}))n).

The proof of Proposition 3.7 follows from Corollary 2.3 and Lemma 3.5. At a high level, we consider dyadic intervals for the threshold function of v⁡(A)v(A), round v⁡(A)v(A) to an appropriate integer lattice (using Lemma 3.5), and then use Corollary 2.3. In order to be in a setting where we can apply Corollary 2.3, we use an idea of Litvak and Tikhomirov [13] – using the Chernoff bound, we restrict ourselves to the event that all but Oξ,γ2.3​(1)O_{\xi,\gamma_{\ref{cor:threshold-inversion}}}(1) rows belong to a well-conditioned multislice corresponding to ξ\xi. We refer the reader to [7, Proposition 4.2] for further details.

3.3. Invertibility on the bulk

We are now ready to state and prove the key result of this section.

Theorem 3.8.

Fix a discrete distribution ξ\xi. For any δ,ρ,ϵ>0\delta,\rho,\epsilon>0, there exists C3.8=C3.8​(ξ,δ,ρ,ϵ)>0C_{\ref{thm:incompressible}}=C_{\ref{thm:incompressible}}(\xi,\delta,\rho,\epsilon)>0 and n3.8​(ξ,δ,ρ,ϵ)≥1n_{\ref{thm:incompressible}}(\xi,\delta,\rho,\epsilon)\geq 1 such that for all n≥n3.8n\geq n_{\ref{thm:incompressible}} and t≥0t\geq 0,

ℙ[infx∈Noncons⁡(δ,ρ)∥Mn(ξ)x∥2≤t/n∧infy∈Cons⁡(δ,ρ)∥yMn(ξ)∥2>C3.8t]≤C3.8t+exp((ϵ−H(p→))n).\mathbb{P}\bigg[\inf_{x\in\operatorname{Noncons}(\delta,\rho)}\lVert M_{n}(\xi)x\rVert_{2}\leq t/\sqrt{n}\wedge\inf_{y\in\operatorname{Cons}(\delta,\rho)}\lVert yM_{n}(\xi)\rVert_{2}>C_{\ref{thm:incompressible}}t\bigg]\leq C_{\ref{thm:incompressible}}t+\exp((\epsilon-H(\vec{p}))n).

Let M:=Mn​(ξ)M:=M_{n}(\xi) for simplicity, and let δ,ρ,ϵ>0\delta,\rho,\epsilon>0 be as in the statement of the theorem. We will denote the columns of MM by M(1),…,M(n)M^{(1)},\dots,M^{(n)}. Also, for each i∈[n]i\in[n], M(−i)M^{(-i)} denotes the subspace spanned by all columns of MM except for M(i)M^{(i)}.

4. Preliminary invertibility estimates

In this short section, we will prove a version of Theorem 1.4 with the weaker singularity estimate (∥p→∥∞+on​(1))n(\lVert\vec{p}\rVert_{\infty}+o_{n}(1))^{n}. This estimate, which generalizes [23, Theorem A], will be used crucially in our refined treatment of invertibility for almost-constant vectors in the next section. The techniques in this section also serve as a gentle warm-up to the next section, where much more involved versions of the arguments are presented.

We begin with the following elementary fact regarding sums of ξ\xi random variables.

Lemma 4.1.

Fix a discrete distribution ξ\xi. There is θ=θ⁡(ξ)>0\theta=\theta(\xi)>0 such that for all x∈𝕊n−1x\in\mathbb{S}^{n-1},

ℒξ​(b1​x1+⋯+bn​xn,θ)≤∥p→∥∞.\mathcal{L}_{\xi}(b_{1}x_{1}+\cdots+b_{n}x_{n},\theta)\leq\lVert\vec{p}\rVert_{\infty}.
Proof.

This is essentially identical to the proof given in [23, Lemma 3.5]. Briefly, if ∥x∥∞≥δ\lVert x\rVert_{\infty}\geq\delta, then we can choose θ\theta small enough (depending on δ\delta and ξ\xi) so the claim is immediate. Otherwise ∥x∥∞<δ\lVert x\rVert_{\infty}<\delta and ∥x∥2=1\lVert x\rVert_{2}=1, in which case the claim follows from Lemma 2.4 as long as δ\delta is sufficiently small depending on ξ\xi. ∎

Combining the above estimate with the second part of Lemma 3.3, we have the following.

Corollary 4.2.

Fix a discrete distribution ξ\xi. For every ϵ>0\epsilon>0, there exists c>0c>0 depending on ϵ\epsilon and ξ\xi such that for any x∈𝕊n−1x\in\mathbb{S}^{n-1} and y∈ℝny\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, we have

ℙ[∥Mn(ξ)x−y∥2≤cn]≤(∥p∥∞+ϵ)n.\mathbb{P}[\lVert M_{n}(\xi)x-y\rVert_{2}\leq c\sqrt{n}]\leq(\lVert p\rVert_{\infty}+\epsilon)^{n}.

Moreover, combining this corollary with the low metric entropy of Cons⁡(δ,ρ)\operatorname{Cons}(\delta,\rho) and Lemma 3.4, we obtain the following (weak) estimate for invertibility on almost-constant vectors.

Corollary 4.3.

Fix a discrete distribution ξ\xi. For every ϵ>0\epsilon>0, there exist δ,ρ,c>0\delta,\rho,c>0 depending on ϵ\epsilon and ξ\xi such that for any y∈ℝny\in\mathbb{R}^{n},

ℙ[infx∈Cons⁡(δ,ρ)∥Mn(ξ)x−y∥2≤cn]≤(∥p∥∞+ϵ)n.\mathbb{P}\bigg[\inf_{x\in\operatorname{Cons}(\delta,\rho)}\lVert M_{n}(\xi)x-y\rVert_{2}\leq c\sqrt{n}\bigg]\leq(\lVert p\rVert_{\infty}+\epsilon)^{n}.

Next, we show that with very high probability, the inverse of any fixed vector is unstructured.

Proposition 4.4.

Fix a discrete distribution ξ\xi. For every ϵ,η>0\epsilon,\eta>0, there exist δ,ρ,L>0\delta,\rho,L>0 depending on ϵ,η,ξ\epsilon,\eta,\xi such that for any y∈ℝny\in\mathbb{R}^{n},

ℙ[∃x∈𝕊n−1:Mn(ξ)x∥y∧(x∈Cons(δ,ρ)∨𝒯ξ(x,L)≥(∥p→∥∞+η)n]≤(∥p→∥∞+ϵ)n.\mathbb{P}\bigg[\exists x\in\mathbb{S}^{n-1}:M_{n}(\xi)x\parallel y\wedge(x\in\operatorname{Cons}(\delta,\rho)\vee\mathcal{T}_{\xi}(x,L)\geq(\lVert\vec{p}\rVert_{\infty}+\eta)^{n}\bigg]\leq(\lVert\vec{p}\rVert_{\infty}+\epsilon)^{n}.
Proof.

This follows essentially from combining Corollary 4.3 with a cruder analogue of Proposition 3.7, the only difference being that we are considering Mn​(ξ)​x|yM_{n}(\xi)x\parallel y for arbitrary y∈ℝny\in\mathbb{R}^{n} as opposed to only y=0y=0.

To handle this last point, we begin by choosing (using Lemma 3.4) a sufficiently large constant KK so that ℰK={∥Mn(ξ)−𝔼[ξ]Jn×n∥≤Kn}\mathcal{E}_{K}=\{\lVert M_{n}(\xi)-\mathbb{E}[\xi]J_{n\times n}\rVert\leq K\sqrt{n}\} satisfies ℙ⁡[ℰKc]≤∥p→∥∞2​n\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{E}_{K}^{c}]\leq\lVert\vec{p}\rVert_{\infty}^{2n}. Then, it suffices to restrict to ℰK\mathcal{E}_{K}. Moreover, by the triangle inequality, we see that on the event ℰK\mathcal{E}_{K}, ∥Mn​(ξ)∥≤K​n+𝔼⁡[ξ]​n\lVert M_{n}(\xi)\rVert\leq K\sqrt{n}+\mathbb{E}[\xi]n, so that in particular, on the event in the proposition (intersected with ℰK\mathcal{E}_{K}), we have that Mn​(ξ)​x=t​y0M_{n}(\xi)x=ty_{0} with y0∈𝕊n−1y_{0}\in\mathbb{S}^{n-1} fixed and for some t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R} with |t|≤K​n+𝔼⁡[ξ]​n|t|\leq K\sqrt{n}+\mathbb{E}[\xi]n.

Now, for the treatment of vectors in Cons⁡(δ,ρ)\operatorname{Cons}(\delta,\rho), we can divide the range of tt into n3n^{3} uniformly spaced intervals, apply Corollary 4.3 with yy equal to the mid-point of an interval times y0y_{0}, and use the union bound. For the treatment of vectors in Noncons⁡(δ,ρ)∧𝒯⁡(x,L)≤(∥p→∥∞+ϵ)n\operatorname{Noncons}(\delta,\rho)\wedge\mathcal{T}(x,L)\leq(\lVert\vec{p}\rVert_{\infty}+\epsilon)^{n}, we divide the range of tt into ∥p→∥∞−2​n\lVert\vec{p}\rVert_{\infty}^{-2n} equally spaced intervals, use a slight generalization of the argument in the proof [7, Proposition 4.2] with MM sufficiently large (depending on ξ\xi) also for yy equal to the mid-point of an interval times y0y_{0}, and finally use the union bound. We leave the details to the interested reader. ∎

Using Corollary 4.3 and Proposition 4.4, we can prove the following weaker version of Theorem 1.4.

Theorem 4.5.

Let ξ\xi be a discrete random variable. For any ϵ>0\epsilon>0, there exist C,n0>0C,n_{0}>0 depending on ξ,ϵ\xi,\epsilon such that for all n≥n0n\geq n_{0} and t≥0t\geq 0,

ℙ[sn(Mn)≤t/n]≤Ct+(∥p→∥∞+ϵ)n.\mathbb{P}[s_{n}(M_{n})\leq t/\sqrt{n}]\leq Ct+(\lVert\vec{p}\rVert_{\infty}+\epsilon)^{n}.
Proof.

The deduction of this theorem follows from the argument in [23, Section 5] with the application of Corollary 4.3 and Proposition 4.4 at the appropriate steps. A more complicated version of this deduction also appears in Section 6, so we omit details. ∎

5. Almost-constant vectors

The goal of this section is to prove Theorem 1.5. The proof is presented at the end of the section and needs a few intermediate steps.

For the proof, we will need to isolate the following natural class of almost-elementary vectors.

Definition 5.1.

(Almost-elementary vectors) For δ>0\delta>0 and i,j∈[n]i,j\in[n], i≠ji\neq j, let

Elemi⁡(δ)\displaystyle\operatorname{Elem}_{i}(\delta) :={x∈𝕊n−1:∥x−ei∥2≤δ},\displaystyle:=\{x\in\mathbb{S}^{n-1}:\lVert x-e_{i}\rVert_{2}\leq\delta\},
Elemi,j⁡(δ)\displaystyle\operatorname{Elem}_{i,j}(\delta) :={x∈𝕊n−1:∥x−(ei−ej)/2∥2≤δ},\displaystyle:=\{x\in\mathbb{S}^{n-1}:\lVert x-(e_{i}-e_{j})/\sqrt{2}\rVert_{2}\leq\delta\},
Elemi,j′⁡(δ)\displaystyle\operatorname{Elem}^{\prime}_{i,j}(\delta) :={x∈𝕊n−1:∥x−(ei+ej)/2∥2≤δ}.\displaystyle:=\{x\in\mathbb{S}^{n-1}:\lVert x-(e_{i}+e_{j})/\sqrt{2}\rVert_{2}\leq\delta\}.

Also, let

Elem⁡(δ)\displaystyle\operatorname{Elem}(\delta) :=⋃i∈[n]Elemi⁡(δ)∪⋃i,j∈[n],i≠jElemi,j⁡(δ),\displaystyle:=\bigcup_{i\in[n]}\operatorname{Elem}_{i}(\delta)\cup\bigcup_{i,j\in[n],i\neq j}\operatorname{Elem}_{i,j}(\delta),
Elem′⁡(δ)\displaystyle\operatorname{Elem}^{\prime}(\delta) :=Elem⁡(δ)∪⋃i,j∈[n],i≠jElemi,j′⁡(δ).\displaystyle:=\operatorname{Elem}(\delta)\cup\bigcup_{i,j\in[n],i\neq j}\operatorname{Elem}^{\prime}_{i,j}(\delta).

For excluding almost-constant vectors which are not almost-elementary, we will need to develop sharp results regarding the Lévy concentration function of discrete random variables.

Proposition 5.2.

Fix a discrete distribution ξ\xi and δ∈(0,1/2)\delta\in(0,1/2). There exists θ=θ⁡(δ,ξ)>0\theta=\theta(\delta,\xi)>0 such that for all x∈𝕊n−1∖Elem′⁡(δ)x\in\mathbb{S}^{n-1}\setminus\operatorname{Elem}^{\prime}(\delta),

ℒξ​(b1​x1+⋯+bn​xn,θ)≤∥p→∥22−θ.\mathcal{L}_{\xi}(b_{1}x_{1}+\cdots+b_{n}x_{n},\theta)\leq\lVert\vec{p}\rVert_{2}^{2}-\theta.
Proof.

Since Elem′⁡(δ)\operatorname{Elem}^{\prime}(\delta) is increasing with δ\delta, it suffices to prove the statement for sufficiently small δ\delta (depending on ξ\xi), which will be chosen during the course of the proof. Moreover, we may assume that |x1|≥|x2|≥⋯≥|xn||x_{1}|\geq|x_{2}|\geq\dots\geq|x_{n}|.

Since x∉Elem1⁡(δ)x\notin\operatorname{Elem}_{1}(\delta), we must have ∥(x2,…,xn)∥2≥δ/2\lVert(x_{2},\dots,x_{n})\rVert_{2}\geq\delta/2. In case |x2|≤δ4|x_{2}|\leq\delta^{4}, then we are done using Lemma 2.4 (cf. [7, Lemma 2.6]) for all sufficiently small δ\delta. Similarly, if ∥(x3,…,xn)∥2≥δ/4\lVert(x_{3},\dots,x_{n})\rVert_{2}\geq\delta/4 and |x3|≤δ4|x_{3}|\leq\delta^{4}, we are done. We now analyze the remaining situations via case analysis.

Case I: δ4≤|x2|<(1−δ5)​|x1|\delta^{4}\leq|x_{2}|<(1-\delta^{5})|x_{1}|. Since ℒξ​(b1​x1+⋯+bn​xn,θ)≤ℒξ​(b1​x1+b2​x2,θ)\mathcal{L}_{\xi}(b_{1}x_{1}+\dots+b_{n}x_{n},\theta)\leq\mathcal{L}_{\xi}(b_{1}x_{1}+b_{2}x_{2},\theta), it suffices to bound the latter. Let ξ′\xi^{\prime} be an independent copy of ξ\xi. For any s∈ℝs\in\mathbb{R}, we have

ℙ[x1ξ+x2ξ′∈[s−c,s+c]]2\displaystyle\mathbb{P}[x_{1}\xi+x_{2}\xi^{\prime}\in[s-c,s+c]]^{2} =(∑aℙ[ξ′=a]ℙ[|ξ−x1−1(s−x2a)|≤c|x1|−1])2\displaystyle=\bigg(\sum_{a}\mathbb{P}[\xi^{\prime}=a]\mathbb{P}[|\xi-x_{1}^{-1}(s-x_{2}a)|\leq c|x_{1}|^{-1}]\bigg)^{2}
≤(∑aℙ[ξ′=a]2)(∑aℙ[|ξ−x1−1(s−x2a)|≤c|x1|−1]2)≤∥p→∥24,\displaystyle\leq\bigg(\sum_{a}\mathbb{P}[\xi^{\prime}=a]^{2}\bigg)\bigg(\sum_{a}\mathbb{P}[|\xi-x_{1}^{-1}(s-x_{2}a)|\leq c|x_{1}|^{-1}]^{2}\bigg)\leq\lVert\vec{p}\rVert_{2}^{4},

Note that, after possibly multiplying by an overall negative sign, u1​ξ1+u2​ξ2+u3​ξ3u_{1}\xi_{1}+u_{2}\xi_{2}+u_{3}\xi_{3} is distributed as either ξ+ξ′+ξ′′\xi+\xi^{\prime}+\xi^{\prime\prime} or ξ+ξ′−ξ′′\xi+\xi^{\prime}-\xi^{\prime\prime}.

Therefore, by our choice of δ\delta and cc, we see that it suffices to show that for all s∈ℝs\in\mathbb{R},

ℙ[ξ1+ξ2+ξ3=s]≤∥p→∥22−cξ,ℙ[ξ1+ξ2−ξ3=s]≤∥p→∥22−cξ,\mathbb{P}[\xi_{1}+\xi_{2}+\xi_{3}=s]\leq\lVert\vec{p}\rVert_{2}^{2}-c_{\xi},\quad\mathbb{P}[\xi_{1}+\xi_{2}-\xi_{3}=s]\leq\lVert\vec{p}\rVert_{2}^{2}-c_{\xi},

for some cξ>0c_{\xi}>0 depending only on ξ\xi. Now for u3∈{±1}u_{3}\in\{\pm 1\}, we have

ℙ[ξ1+ξ2+u3ξ3=s]2\displaystyle\mathbb{P}[\xi_{1}+\xi_{2}+u_{3}\xi_{3}=s]^{2} =(∑aℙ[ξ3=a]ℙ[ξ1+ξ2=s−u3a])2\displaystyle=\bigg(\sum_{a}\mathbb{P}[\xi_{3}=a]\mathbb{P}[\xi_{1}+\xi_{2}=s-u_{3}a]\bigg)^{2}
≤(∑aℙ[ξ3=a]2)(∑aℙ[ξ1+ξ2=s−u3a]2)\displaystyle\leq\bigg(\sum_{a}\mathbb{P}[\xi_{3}=a]^{2}\bigg)\bigg(\sum_{a}\mathbb{P}[\xi_{1}+\xi_{2}=s-u_{3}a]^{2}\bigg)
≤(∑aℙ[ξ3=a]2)(∑a′∈supp⁡(ξ1+ξ2)ℙ[ξ1+ξ2=a′]2)\displaystyle\leq\bigg(\sum_{a}\mathbb{P}[\xi_{3}=a]^{2}\bigg)\bigg(\sum_{a^{\prime}\in\operatorname{supp}(\xi_{1}+\xi_{2})}\mathbb{P}[\xi_{1}+\xi_{2}=a^{\prime}]^{2}\bigg)
≤∥p→∥24,\displaystyle\leq\lVert\vec{p}\rVert_{2}^{4},

where the first line is by definition, the second line is Cauchy-Schwarz, and the last line follows by Young’s convolution inequality. To obtain the inequality with a positive constant cξ>0c_{\xi}>0, we note that equality cannot hold in the third line since supp⁡(ξ1+ξ2)\operatorname{supp}(\xi_{1}+\xi_{2}) has strictly more positive atoms than supp⁡(ξ)\operatorname{supp}(\xi) (since ξ\xi is supported on at least 22 points), and this leads to the desired improvement since ξ\xi has finite support. ∎

When ξ\xi is not a translate of an origin-symmetric distribution, the above result can be strengthened.

Proposition 5.3.

Fix a discrete distribution ξ\xi and δ∈(0,1/2)\delta\in(0,1/2). Suppose that ξ\xi is not a translate of any origin-symmetric distribution. Then, there exists θ=θ⁡(δ,ξ)>0\theta=\theta(\delta,\xi)>0 such that for all x∈𝕊n−1∖Elem⁡(δ)x\in\mathbb{S}^{n-1}\setminus\operatorname{Elem}(\delta),

ℒξ​(b1​x1+⋯+bn​xn,θ)≤∥p→∥22−θ.\mathcal{L}_{\xi}(b_{1}x_{1}+\cdots+b_{n}x_{n},\theta)\leq\lVert\vec{p}\rVert_{2}^{2}-\theta.
Proof.

As before, since Elem⁡(δ)\operatorname{Elem}(\delta) is increasing with δ\delta, it suffices to prove the statement for sufficiently small δ\delta depending on ξ\xi. By Proposition 5.2, we can choose θ=θ⁡(δ,ξ)>0\theta=\theta(\delta,\xi)>0 such that for all x∈𝕊n−1∖Elem⁡(δ)x\in\mathbb{S}^{n-1}\setminus\operatorname{Elem}(\delta),

ℒξ​(b1​x1+⋯+bn​xn,θ)≤∥p→∥22−θ.\mathcal{L}_{\xi}(b_{1}x_{1}+\cdots+b_{n}x_{n},\theta)\leq\lVert\vec{p}\rVert_{2}^{2}-\theta.

Hence, it remains to prove the result for x∈Elem′⁡(δ)∖Elem⁡(δ)x\in\operatorname{Elem}^{\prime}(\delta)\setminus\operatorname{Elem}(\delta). By symmetry, it suffices to consider x∈Elem1,2′⁡(δ)x\in\operatorname{Elem}^{\prime}_{1,2}(\delta). We will bound ℒξ​(b1​x1+b2​x2,θ)\mathcal{L}_{\xi}(b_{1}x_{1}+b_{2}x_{2},\theta).

We use an argument similar to Case IV of the proof of Proposition 5.2. Let mξ′>0m^{\prime}_{\xi}>0 be the smallest positive real for which supp⁡(ξ)⊆[−mξ′,mξ′]\operatorname{supp}(\xi)\subseteq[-m^{\prime}_{\xi},m^{\prime}_{\xi}]. We have

ℙ[x1ξ1+x2ξ2∈[s−c,s+c]]≤ℙ[12(ξ1+ξ2)∈[s−c−2mξ′δ,s+c+2mξ′δ]].\mathbb{P}[x_{1}\xi_{1}+x_{2}\xi_{2}\in[s-c,s+c]]\leq\mathbb{P}\bigg[\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(\xi_{1}+\xi_{2})\in[s-c-2m^{\prime}_{\xi}\delta,s+c+2m^{\prime}_{\xi}\delta]\bigg].

Once again, by choosing δ\delta and cc sufficiently small (depending on ξ\xi), we may assume that 2​(c+2​mξ′​δ)2(c+2m^{\prime}_{\xi}\delta) is smaller than the minimum distance between two distinct atoms in supp⁡(ξ+ξ′)\operatorname{supp}(\xi+\xi^{\prime}), where ξ,ξ′\xi,\xi^{\prime} are independent copies of ξ\xi. With this choice of δ\delta and cc, the problem reduces to showing that there exists some cξ>0c_{\xi}>0 depending only on ξ\xi such that for all s∈ℝs\in\mathbb{R},

ℙ[ξ1+ξ2=s]≤∥p→∥22−cξ.\mathbb{P}[\xi_{1}+\xi_{2}=s]\leq\lVert\vec{p}\rVert_{2}^{2}-c_{\xi}.

We have

ℙ[ξ1+ξ2=s]=∑aℙ[ξ1=a]ℙ[ξ2=s−a]≤(∑aℙ[ξ1=a]2)1/2(∑aℙ[ξ2=s−a]2)1/2≤∥p→∥22,\mathbb{P}[\xi_{1}+\xi_{2}=s]=\sum_{a}\mathbb{P}[\xi_{1}=a]\mathbb{P}[\xi_{2}=s-a]\leq\bigg(\sum_{a}\mathbb{P}[\xi_{1}=a]^{2}\bigg)^{1/2}\bigg(\sum_{a}\mathbb{P}[\xi_{2}=s-a]^{2}\bigg)^{1/2}\leq\lVert\vec{p}\rVert_{2}^{2},

where the first inequality is Cauchy-Schwarz. To obtain the improved inequality with cξ>0c_{\xi}>0, we note that equality can hold in both inequalities if and only if ℙ[ξ1=a]=ℙ[ξ2=s−a]\mathbb{P}[\xi_{1}=a]=\mathbb{P}[\xi_{2}=s-a], which implies that ξ\xi is a shift (by s/2s/2) of an origin-symmetric random variable. Since we have assumed that ξ\xi is not a shift of an origin-symmetric random variable, we see that equality cannot hold, and using that the support of ξ\xi is finite, we can conclude. ∎

Using the preceding lemmas, and exploiting the low metric entropy of Cons⁡(δ,ρ)\operatorname{Cons}(\delta,\rho) along with Lemma 3.4, we obtain the following corollary. Note that since ξ\xi may not have mean 00, one must perform the standard trick of densifying the net of these vectors along the direction 1n1_{n} (see [23, Proposition 3.6]). We refer the reader to [7, Proposition 2.7] for the (standard) details.

Corollary 5.4.

Fix a discrete distribution ξ\xi. For all δ′>0\delta^{\prime}>0, there exist δ,ρ,ϵ′,n0>0\delta,\rho,\epsilon^{\prime},n_{0}>0, depending on ξ\xi and δ′\delta^{\prime}, such that for all n≥n0n\geq n_{0},

ℙ[∃x∈Cons(δ,ρ)∖Elem′(δ′):∥Mn(ξ)x∥2≤ϵ′n]≤(∥p→∥22−ϵ′)n.\mathbb{P}[\exists x\in\operatorname{Cons}(\delta,\rho)\setminus\operatorname{Elem}^{\prime}(\delta^{\prime}):\lVert M_{n}(\xi)x\rVert_{2}\leq\epsilon^{\prime}\sqrt{n}]\leq(\lVert\vec{p}\rVert_{2}^{2}-\epsilon^{\prime})^{n}.

Further, if ξ\xi is not a shift of any origin-symmetric random variable, then the same conclusion holds with Elem⁡(δ′)\operatorname{Elem}(\delta^{\prime}) instead of Elem′⁡(δ′)\operatorname{Elem}^{\prime}(\delta^{\prime}).

Given the previous corollary, it remains to analyze vectors in Elem′⁡(δ′)\operatorname{Elem}^{\prime}(\delta^{\prime}) (or only in Elem⁡(δ′)\operatorname{Elem}(\delta^{\prime}) if ξ\xi is not a shift of any origin-symmetric random variable), which is the content of the remainder of this section.

5.1. Two columns

We first handle vectors in Elemi,j⁡(δ′)\operatorname{Elem}_{i,j}(\delta^{\prime}). By the invariance of the distribution of Mn​(ξ)M_{n}(\xi) under permuting columns, it suffices to analyze vectors in Elem1,2⁡(δ′)\operatorname{Elem}_{1,2}(\delta^{\prime}). We show the following.

Proposition 5.5.

Fix a discrete distribution ξ\xi. There exist δ′,η,n0>0\delta^{\prime},\eta,n_{0}>0 depending on ξ\xi such that for all n≥n0n\geq n_{0} and t≤1t\leq 1,

ℙ[∃x∈Elem1,2(δ′):∥Mn(ξ)x∥2≤t]≤∥p→∥22​n+(∥p→∥22−η)n+texp(−ηn).\mathbb{P}[\exists x\in\operatorname{Elem}_{1,2}(\delta^{\prime}):\lVert M_{n}(\xi)x\rVert_{2}\leq t]\leq\lVert\vec{p}\rVert_{2}^{2n}+(\lVert\vec{p}\rVert_{2}^{2}-\eta)^{n}+t\exp(-\eta n).

We will need the following preliminary lemma, which essentially follows from the seminal work of Rudelson and Vershynin [19]. Since we were not able to locate the statement we need in the literature, we provide details below and in [7, Lemma 2.9].

Lemma 5.6.

Fix S,s>0S,s>0. There exist C′,c′,n0>0C^{\prime},c^{\prime},n_{0}>0 depending on s,Ss,S such that the following holds. For all n≥n0n\geq n_{0}, any v∈ℝnv\in\mathbb{R}^{n} with ∥v∥2≥1\lVert v\rVert_{2}\geq 1, any κ∈(0,1)\kappa\in(0,1), and all t≤1t\leq 1, we have

ℙ[∃x∈ℝn−1:∥Ax−v∥2≤t]≤C′n3texp(κn)+exp(−c′n)exp(κn),\mathbb{P}[\exists x\in\mathbb{R}^{n-1}:\lVert Ax-v\rVert_{2}\leq t]\leq C^{\prime}n^{3}\sqrt{t}\exp(\kappa n)+\exp(-c^{\prime}n)\exp(\kappa n),

where AA is an n×(n−1)n\times(n-1) random matrix, each of whose entries is an independent random variable with sub-Gaussian norm at most SS, and such that all but a collection of κ​n\kappa n specified entries have variance at least ss.

Proof.

By the law of total probability, it suffices to assume that the κ​n\kappa n specified entries are deterministic, and take the values a1,…,aκ​na_{1},\dots,a_{\kappa n}. Consider the n×(n−1)n\times(n-1) random matrix A′A^{\prime}, which has the same distribution as AA, except for the κ​n\kappa n specified entries, which are now replaced by a1+b1,…,aκ​n+bκ​na_{1}+b_{1},\dots,a_{\kappa n}+b_{\kappa n}, where b1,…,bκ​nb_{1},\dots,b_{\kappa n} are independent Ber⁡(1/2)\operatorname{Ber}(1/2) random variables.

From a slight generalization of [7, Lemma 2.9] (specifically, one should replace the application of [19] with an inhomogeneous version due to [15] and replace 2−c​n2^{-cn} by tt, see the proof of Lemma 5.9), we get that there exist C′,c′,n0C^{\prime},c^{\prime},n_{0} depending on s,Ss,S such that for all n≥n0n\geq n_{0}, for any v∈ℝnv\in\mathbb{R}^{n} with ∥v∥2≥1\lVert v\rVert_{2}\geq 1, and for all t≥1t\geq 1, we have

ℙ[∃x∈ℝn−1:∥A′x−v∥2≤t]≤C′n3t+exp(−c′n).\mathbb{P}[\exists x\in\mathbb{R}^{n-1}:\lVert A^{\prime}x-v\rVert_{2}\leq t]\leq C^{\prime}n^{3}\sqrt{t}+\exp(-c^{\prime}n).

The conclusion now follows since, with probability 2−κ​n2^{-\kappa n}, b1=⋯=bκ​n=0b_{1}=\dots=b_{\kappa n}=0. ∎

We now prove Proposition 5.5.

Proof of Proposition 5.5.

By Lemma 3.4, we can choose K>0K>0 depending on ξ\xi such that ℙ⁡[ℰK]≤∥p→∥23​n\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{E}_{K}]\leq\lVert\vec{p}\rVert_{2}^{3n}, where

ℰK:={∥Mn(ξ)−𝔼[ξ]Jn×n∥≤Kn}.\mathcal{E}_{K}:=\{\lVert M_{n}(\xi)-\mathbb{E}[\xi]J_{n\times n}\rVert\leq K\sqrt{n}\}.

For δ′∈(0,1/4)\delta^{\prime}\in(0,1/4), which will be chosen later in terms of ξ\xi, let

ℰ:={∃x∈𝔹2n​(e1,δ′)∩𝕊n−1:∥Mn​(ξ)​Q​x∥2≤t},\mathcal{E}:=\{\exists x\in\mathbb{B}_{2}^{n}(e_{1},\delta^{\prime})\cap\mathbb{S}^{n-1}:\lVert M_{n}(\xi)Qx\rVert_{2}\leq t\},

where QQ is the rotation matrix whose bottom-right (n−2)×(n−2)(n-2)\times(n-2) minor is the identity matrix, and the top-left 2×22\times 2 minor is the rotation matrix given by

[1212−1212].\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}&\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}&\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{bmatrix}.

Up to scaling δ′\delta^{\prime} by a constant factor, this is clearly equivalent to the event that we wish to bound.

Note that on the event ℰ\mathcal{E}, there exists some vector y=e1+u∈ℝny=e_{1}+u\in\mathbb{R}^{n} with u1=0u_{1}=0 and ∥u∥2≤4​δ′\lVert u\rVert_{2}\leq 4\delta^{\prime} such that

∥Mn​(ξ)​Q​y∥2≤2​t.\lVert M_{n}(\xi)Qy\rVert_{2}\leq 2t.

Let u′=(u2,…,un)∈ℝn−1u^{\prime}=(u_{2},\ldots,u_{n})\in\mathbb{R}^{n-1}, let M~(1)\widetilde{M}^{(1)} be the first column of Mn​(ξ)​QM_{n}(\xi)Q, and let M~(−1)\widetilde{M}^{(-1)} denote the n×(n−1)n\times(n-1) matrix obtained by removing this column. Then, on the event ℰ∧ℰK\mathcal{E}\wedge\mathcal{E}_{K}, we have

∥M~(1)−𝔼⁡[ξ]​Jn×n−1​u′∥2\displaystyle\lVert\widetilde{M}^{(1)}-\mathbb{E}[\xi]J_{n\times n-1}u^{\prime}\rVert_{2} ≤∥M~(1)+M~(−1)​u′∥2+∥(M~(−1)−𝔼⁡[ξ]​Jn×n−1)​u′∥2\displaystyle\leq\lVert\widetilde{M}^{(1)}+\widetilde{M}^{(-1)}u^{\prime}\rVert_{2}+\lVert(\widetilde{M}^{(-1)}-\mathbb{E}[\xi]J_{n\times n-1})u^{\prime}\rVert_{2}
≤2​t+K​n⋅4​δ′\displaystyle\leq 2t+K\sqrt{n}\cdot 4\delta^{\prime}
≤8​K​δ′​n\displaystyle\leq 8K\delta^{\prime}\sqrt{n}

for all sufficiently large nn, since t≤1t\leq 1.

The key point is the following. Let Ξ:=supp⁡(ξ−ξ′)/2⊆ℝ\Xi:=\operatorname{supp}(\xi-\xi^{\prime})/\sqrt{2}\subseteq\mathbb{R}. Let

𝒞:={a∈Ξn:∃λ∈ℝ​ with ​∥a−λ​1n∥2≤8​K​δ′​n},\mathcal{C}:=\{a\in\Xi^{n}:\exists\lambda\in\mathbb{R}\text{ with }\lVert a-\lambda 1_{n}\rVert_{2}\leq 8K\delta^{\prime}\sqrt{n}\},

and for κ=κ⁡(δ′,ξ)>0\kappa=\kappa(\delta^{\prime},\xi)>0, to be chosen later depending on δ′,ξ\delta^{\prime},\xi, and for z∈Ξz\in\Xi, let

𝒞z:=𝒞∩{a∈ℝn:|supp⁡(a−z​1n)|≤κ​n}.\mathcal{C}_{z}:=\mathcal{C}\cap\{a\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:|\operatorname{supp}(a-z1_{n})|\leq\kappa n\}.

It is easy to see that

𝒞⊆⋃z∈Ξ𝒞z\mathcal{C}\subseteq\bigcup_{z\in\Xi}\mathcal{C}_{z}

for an appropriate choice of κ\kappa which goes to 00 as δ′\delta^{\prime} goes to 00. Furthermore,

ℙ[M~(1)∈𝒞z]≤ℙ[(ξ−ξ′)/2=z]nexp(cκ,δ′,ξn),\mathbb{P}[\widetilde{M}^{(1)}\in\mathcal{C}_{z}]\leq\mathbb{P}[(\xi-\xi^{\prime})/\sqrt{2}=z]^{n}\exp(c_{\kappa,\delta^{\prime},\xi}n),

where cκ,δ′,ξ>0c_{\kappa,\delta^{\prime},\xi}>0 goes to 00 as κ,δ′\kappa,\delta^{\prime} go to 00. Therefore, we have

ℙ[M~(1)∈𝒞]≤∥p→∥22​nexp(2cκ,δ′,ξn), and \mathbb{P}[\widetilde{M}^{(1)}\in\mathcal{C}]\leq\lVert\vec{p}\rVert_{2}^{2n}\exp(2c_{\kappa,\delta^{\prime},\xi}n),\text{ and }
ℙ[M~(1)∈𝒞∖𝒞0]≤(∥p→∥22−cξ)n\mathbb{P}[\widetilde{M}^{(1)}\in\mathcal{C}\setminus\mathcal{C}_{0}]\leq(\lVert\vec{p}\rVert_{2}^{2}-c_{\xi})^{n}

for some cξ>0c_{\xi}>0 depending only on ξ\xi, provided that δ′\delta^{\prime} (hence κ\kappa) is chosen sufficiently small. Here, for the second inequality, we have used that by Cauchy-Schwarz (as in the proof of Proposition 5.2), the unique most probable atom of (ξ−ξ′)/2(\xi-\xi^{\prime})/\sqrt{2} is at 00, and is ∥p→∥22\lVert\vec{p}\rVert_{2}^{2}, so that any other atom in Ξ\Xi has probability at most ∥p→∥22−2​cξ\lVert\vec{p}\rVert_{2}^{2}-2c_{\xi} for some cξ>0c_{\xi}>0.

So far, we have shown that for all κ\kappa and δ′\delta^{\prime} sufficiently small (depending on ξ\xi), we have

ℙ⁡[ℰ]\displaystyle\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{E}] ≤∥p→∥23​n+∑a∈𝒞ℙ[M~(1)=a]ℙ[∃u′∈ℝn−1:∥M~(−1)u′+a∥2≤2t|M~(1)]\displaystyle\leq\lVert\vec{p}\rVert_{2}^{3n}+\sum_{a\in\mathcal{C}}\mathbb{P}[\widetilde{M}^{(1)}=a]\mathbb{P}[\exists u^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{n-1}:\lVert\widetilde{M}^{(-1)}u^{\prime}+a\rVert_{2}\leq 2t|\widetilde{M}^{(1)}]
≤∥p→∥23​n+(∥p→∥22−cξ)n+∑a∈𝒞0ℙ[M~(1)=a]ℙ[∃u′∈ℝn−1:∥M~(−1)u′+a∥2≤2t|M~(1)].\displaystyle\leq\lVert\vec{p}\rVert_{2}^{3n}+(\lVert\vec{p}\rVert_{2}^{2}-c_{\xi})^{n}+\sum_{a\in\mathcal{C}_{0}}\mathbb{P}[\widetilde{M}^{(1)}=a]\mathbb{P}[\exists u^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{n-1}:\lVert\widetilde{M}^{(-1)}u^{\prime}+a\rVert_{2}\leq 2t|\widetilde{M}^{(1)}].

We proceed to bound the third term in the above sum.

Case I: If a=0a=0, we have ℙ[M~(1)=0]=∥p∥22​n\mathbb{P}[\widetilde{M}^{(1)}=0]=\lVert p\rVert_{2}^{2n}.

Case II: If a≠0a\neq 0, we have in particular that ∥a∥2≥hξ>0\lVert a\rVert_{2}\geq h_{\xi}>0. The crucial observation is the following. Given M~(1)=a\widetilde{M}^{(1)}=a, the entries of the first column of M~(−1)\widetilde{M}^{(-1)} are independent random variables, each of which is distributed as the sum of two i.i.d. copies of ξ/2\xi/\sqrt{2}, conditioned on knowing their difference.
